Western corella (Cacatua pastinator) hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days]. This incubation duration is typical for medium-sized cockatoos and reflects the altricial developmental mode characteristic of the Cacatuidae. At the moment of hatching, the neonate carries a modest body mass, with field measurements indicating that the initial wet weight is approximately 20.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 20.6 grams]. This small starting mass, less than four percent of the eventual adult size, underscores the heavy reliance on biparental provisioning during the subsequent nestling phase. The parents must deliver substantial food resources to enable rapid somatic growth, a critical period during which the chick transforms from a near-naked, helpless hatchling into a fully feathered and mobile fledgling. The energetic demands on the breeding pair are therefore considerable, and successful broods depend on predictable food availability in the surrounding woodland and pastoral habitats that this species inhabits.

Under the warm thermal regime typical of the species' active physiological state, which averages 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a series of developmental milestones is reached in predictable succession. The first of these is fledging, when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight at approximately 60 days after hatching [tx = approximately 60 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This period of parental dependency is relatively prolonged among parrots, reflecting the need for extensive feather development and neuromuscular coordination before independence can be attempted. Following fledging, the juvenile enters a period of continued growth and learning, refining foraging skills under the tutelage of its parents. Sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to produce gametes, is attained considerably later at around 180 days after hatching [tp = around 180 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This delay between fledging and reproductive maturation ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient body reserves and experience to successfully compete for nesting hollows and mates.

Adult body mass in the Western corella exhibits a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism, a common pattern among cockatoos where males tend to be slightly larger than females. For adult females, the ultimate wet weight attained at full somatic maturity averages 551 grams [Wwi = 551 grams], whereas adult males reach a corresponding mass of 610 grams [Wwi = 610 grams]. This difference of nearly sixty grams is thought to reflect selective pressures related to male-male competition for access to nesting sites and for dominance during foraging flocks. The larger body size in males may confer advantages in aggressive encounters, allowing them to secure higher-quality hollows in eucalypt woodland. Conversely, the slightly smaller size of females may reduce their absolute energetic requirements during the demanding incubation and early chick-rearing periods. These mass values were compiled from multiple field studies across the species' range in southwestern Australia and are consistent with measurements reported for other members of the genus Cacatua.

Reproductive output in the Western corella is limited by both clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts within a single breeding season. Under the optimal thermal conditions typical of an actively incubating adult (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), females typically produce a clutch of 1 to 4 eggs per breeding attempt [N_R_i = 1 to 4 eggs per breeding attempt], with the modal clutch size most frequently being two or three eggs, and they raise approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year]. Field records from the wheatbelt region indicate that most breeding pairs initiate their first brood at an age of 2 years since birth [tR = 2 years since birth], a relatively early onset of reproduction for a bird of this size at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This early first breeding event contrasts with the longer prereproductive periods observed in larger cockatoo species and may reflect the trade-off between body size and life-history pace.

Longevity data for the Western corella indicate a remarkably extended maximum lifespan, with the oldest documented wild individuals reaching an age of approximately 26.3 years [am = approximately 26.3 years] under the typical physiological temperature regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This substantial lifespan is characteristic of the Psittaciformes order, where many species exhibit slow senescence rates and prolonged reproductive windows. For the Western corella, the capacity for such longevity is coupled with a relatively low annual adult mortality once individuals have survived the vulnerable juvenile and subadult stages. The species' ability to exploit both natural eucalypt seeds and agricultural grain resources has likely contributed to its demographic resilience, buffering populations against periodic food shortages that might otherwise truncate lifespan. This combination of early reproduction, modest clutch sizes, and extended adult survival defines a life-history strategy well-suited to the unpredictable Mediterranean climate of its native range.
